title: Anomalous magneto-optical response at $\mathrm{RuO_2 / WSe_2}$ van der Waals interface
authors: Muhammad Hassan Shaikh, Abhijith Puthiya Veettil, Collin Maurtua, Dai Q. Ho, Subhash Bhatt, David T. Plouff, Malitha Gulawita, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, John Q. Xiao, Anderson Janotti, Chitraleema Chakraborty
abstract: Ruthenium dioxide ($\mathrm{RuO_2}$) has been proposed as an altermagnetic candidate, although its magnetic ground state remains controversial. Here, we probe weak interfacial magnetic states at the surface of (001)-oriented $\mathrm{RuO_2}$ films using the magnetic proximity effect (MPE) in a van der Waals heterostructure consisting of monolayer tungsten diselenide ($\mathrm{WSe_2}$) atop $\mathrm{RuO_2}$. Temperature-dependent magneto-optical spectroscopy reveals an anomalous excitonic energy shift and a deviation from conventional Varshni behavior below 55 K that are absent in an encapsulated $\mathrm{WSe_2}$ control sample. The anomalous shift reverses sign upon field cooling with opposite magnetic field polarity, indicating a magnetic origin. Polarization-resolved measurements further show a nearly field-independent and fluctuating valley splitting in $\mathrm{WSe_2 / RuO_2}$ in strong contrast to the conventional linear Zeeman splitting observed in the control bare $\mathrm{WSe_2}$ sample. These results suggest that the valley states are governed predominantly by interfacial exchange fields associated with weak surface magnetic states in $\mathrm{RuO_2}$, which do not produce a conventional linear Zeeman response within the applied magnetic field range. Importantly, this approach enables direct optical probing of emergent surface magnetism without introducing an additional ferromagnetic layer, positioning MPE-based optical probing as a tool for investigating weak surface magnetism and offering new possibilities for studying magnetic materials with controversial magnetic states.
summary: The research investigates weak surface magnetism in $\mathrm{RuO_2}$ by studying its interaction with monolayer $\mathrm{WSe_2}$ using magneto-optical spectroscopy. Anomalous energy shifts and unique field responses observed below 55 K strongly suggest that the valley states are governed by interfacial magnetic exchange fields. This establishes a powerful, non-invasive optical tool for characterizing subtle magnetism in challenging material systems.
main_problem: The study aims to probe weak interfacial magnetic states at the surface of $\mathrm{RuO_2}$ using optical techniques, circumventing the controversy surrounding its bulk magnetic ground state.
main_result: Anomalous magneto-optical responses, including temperature-dependent energy shifts and unusual valley splitting behavior in $\mathrm{WSe_2}$, were observed, suggesting that interfacial exchange fields govern the electronic structure via weak surface magnetism.
method: Temperature-dependent magneto-optical spectroscopy (magneto-photoluminescence) was performed on a van der Waals heterostructure ($\mathrm{WSe_2}$ atop $\mathrm{RuO_2}$) compared to an encapsulated control sample, using applied out-of-plane magnetic fields.
model_or_system: The physical system is the $\mathrm{WSe_2/RuO_2}$ van der Waals heterostructure. The investigation focuses on emergent surface magnetism in $\mathrm{RuO_2}$ and its influence on the excitonic states of monolayer $\mathrm{WSe_2}$.
key_observables: Anomalous excitonic energy shift, deviation from Varshni behavior below 55 K, and field-dependent valley splitting ($\sigma^+$ vs. $\sigma^-$ polarization measurements).
important_parameters: Temperature ($T < 55$ K), applied magnetic field (up to $\pm 6 	ext{ T}$ out-of-plane).
main_assumptions: The anomalous optical response is attributed to interfacial exchange fields associated with weak surface magnetic states in $\mathrm{RuO_2}$, rather than conventional Zeeman splitting or non-magnetic effects.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temperature dependence of the excitonic peak energy, showing a deviation from Varshni behavior only in the $\mathrm{WSe_2/RuO_2}$ sample below $T_1$. They also show polarization-resolved measurements demonstrating negligible Zeeman splitting in the heterostructure compared to the control.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of probing weak surface magnetism, details the use of magneto-optical spectroscopy on the $\mathrm{WSe_2/RuO_2}$ system, presents evidence for anomalous temperature and field dependencies (deviation from Varshni behavior), and concludes by positioning this technique as a tool for studying emergent interfacial magnetism.
why_interesting: This work provides an optical method to probe weak magnetic interactions at interfaces without requiring the deposition of an additional ferromagnetic layer, which is highly relevant for understanding correlated electron systems in 2D heterostructures.

figures.caption: Figure 1: (a) Schematic of a heterostructure consisting of a monolayer WSe2 atop a RuO2 (001) film, with h-BN encapsulation on top, used for surface magnetism studies. (b) Schematic of the control sample: a monolayer WSe2 encapsulated by h-BN on both top and bottom. (c,d) Room-temperature PL spectra of monolayer WSe2 from the devices shown in (a) and (b), respectively. The dotted lines represent Lorentzian fits for A-excitons (yellow) and trions (cyan) used to extract peak energies. The peak energy of WSe2 atop RuO2 is blue-shifted by 3.8±0.1 meV compared to the encapsulated bare WSe2.

Figure 2: (a) Peak energy of WSe2 as a function of temperature. Blue squares represent the peak energy of WSe2 atop RuO2 in the presence of a 6 T out-of-plane magnetic field. Purple squares represent the peak energy of encapsulated WSe2 without any applied magnetic field. Solid lines are Varshni fits for encapsulated WSe2 (purple) and WSe2 atop RuO2 (blue). Encapsulated WSe2 peak energy follows the Varshni fit across the entire temperature range, while WSe2 atop RuO2 follows it until 55 K (T1). Beyond that, the Varshni behavior is shown by the blue dotted line. Figure 3: (a) Peak energy of WSe2 atop RuO2 as a function of temperature in the presence of ±6 T. The separation between the peak energies for positive and negative fields is minimal between 55 K (T1) and 33 K (T2), and increases below T2. (b) Magnitude of the energy difference between WSe2 atop RuO2 and encapsulated WSe2 as a function of temperature below T2 in the presence of ±6 T.

Figure 4: (a), (b), and (c) show schematics of valley-specific transitions in WSe2 and a comparison between right-handed and left-handed emission energies (E(σ+) and E(σ−)) for magnetic fields greater than, equal to, and less than zero, respectively. (d) Valley splitting energy magnitude (δE) as a function of magnetic field for encapsulated WSe2 (blue diamonds) and WSe2 atop RuO2 (purple diamonds). The red line shows the linear fit for the Zeeman splitting behavior of encapsulated WSe2, from which the extracted g-factor was found to be 4.07 ± 0.24. Spintronics.note: The study uses magneto-optical spectroscopy to probe weak surface magnetism ($\mathrm{RuO_2}$) influencing excitonic states in a heterostructure ($\mathrm{WSe_2}$), directly connecting quantum optics (PL/spectroscopy) with magnetic phenomena (magneto-optical response).
